incarcerated without facing trial or being granted bail. The fact that they have been charged with terror
offences under the UAPA, with stringent bail conditions, should have been reason to expedite their
trial. In the last three years and more, instead, their bail pleas were heard by the Delhi High Court, the
verdicts reserved, only for the judges in question to retire or be transferred. Last week, before the
Supreme Court of India, the Delhi Police opposed bail once again, claiming in their affidavit that the
accused orchestrated the anti-CAA protests and the Delhi riots of 2020 in a “criminal conspiracy
hatched for…. achieving the final ‘regime change’ goal”. The “regime change” accusation, evidently
an exercise in spectre-mongering, is a worrying escalation in how the ruling establishment frames
protest and dissent — in order to delegitimise and criminalise it.

of a democracy. Even after the Emergency, an authoritarian regime was ousted at the ballot box. Unlike
some of its neighbours, citizens in this country have the right to dissent and express their grievances
in elections that are regarded as free and fair. In recent years, however, those who protest against the
government have been demonised — as “anti-national” now, as “urban Naxals” then. The Delhi Police
seek to add “regime change” to this list of loose labels that shrink the spaces for dialogue and debate
and imbue democratic disagreement with sinister intent.

protest a variety of issues. Protesters have also been arrested in the past. But what makes the case
against Khalid, Imam and others more disturbing was articulated by the Delhi HC bench that granted
bail to Khalid’s co-accused, Natasha Narwal, Devangana Kalita and Asif Tanha in 2021: “… it
seems that in its anxiety to suppress dissent, in the mind of the state, the line between the
constitutionally guaranteed right to protest and terrorist activity seems to be getting somewhat
blurred. If this mindset gains traction, it would be a sad day for democracy.”

questions.stimulus:
We are living in an age that celebrates being busy as if it were a badge of honour. The most common
answer to “How are you?” is no longer “I am well,” but “I am busy.” To be occupied every hour of
the day is seen as proof of importance. To be constantly working is admirable. To slow down is
questionable. And to do nothing at all is almost venial. The 24×7 productivity culture did not arrive
suddenly. It grew quietly alongside technological progress. Machines were invented to reduce human
effort.


Computers promised efficiency. The internet connected the world. Smartphones placed the office
inside our pockets. In theory, these innovations were meant to give us more time. In practice, they have
stretched the working day into every corner of our lives. Work no longer ends at sunset. E-mails arrive
at midnight. Messages demand instant replies. Even holidays are filled with digital interruptions. We
carry our responsibilities everywhere like invisible luggage. The body may rest, but the mind rarely
does. Gradually, something deeper has changed within us. Productivity has become more than a


necessity; it has become a moral value. We feel proud when we are exhausted. We speak of “grind”
and “hustle” as virtues. A day filled with tasks feels meaningful. A day of quiet reflection feels
suspicious. Rest begins to carry guilt.


This guilt is subtle but powerful. When we sit without doing anything, a voice inside asks, “Shouldn’t
you be working?” When we take a break, we feel the need to justify it. Even leisure must prove its
usefulness. We exercise not for joy but for measurable fitness goals. We read not for pleasure but to
complete yearly targets. Time with friends becomes “networking.” Conversations become
opportunities. We measure even human connection in terms of usefulness. The simple joy of sitting
together without purpose starts to feel inefficient. Yet it is precisely these purposeless moments that
build intimacy and trust. Mental health also pays a price. Burnout is no longer rare; it is common.
Anxiety rises. Attention spans shrink. Sleep becomes shorter and lighter. If we continue to value
ourselves solely by what we produce, we risk becoming efficient machines rather than thoughtful
human beings. Perhaps the most courageous act in our age is simply to pause. To sit quietly without
creating content. To enjoy without performing. To rest without guilt. In doing so, we do not lose time
– we reclaim our humanity.

The US-China rivalry has increasingly been characterised as the Group of Two. There are expectations
and fears in some quarters that the G2 implies a system in which the US and China strike bargains and
collude to manage the world on their own terms. However, the structural competition between the two
— both seeking dominance in military, advanced technologies, trade networks, and supply chains —
is too intense for them to enter a permanently cooperative relationship that marginalises other powers.


The Busan summit led to a deal under which China would defer export controls on rare earths and
increase agricultural purchases from the US, while Trump reduced tariffs on Chinese imports. Yet the
truce is temporary, allowing the US and China to undo the damage from the trade war they themselves
escalated, and is due for renegotiation in a year. What can be expected of the G2, therefore, is a
dynamic equilibrium swinging between confrontation and cooperation. Still, it is essential to recognise


that China is, indeed, a great power. Its influence is everywhere: Manufactured products, smartphones,
green energy, and trade. China’s control over rare earths gives it significant leverage in international
affairs, and the technology gap between Washington and Beijing is evidently shrinking. China’s power
is only going to grow.


For India, China remains its foremost strategic rival. Beijing’s adventurism on the border has grown;
India runs a trade deficit of over $100 billion, and the China-Pakistan nexus persists. The challenge
for India, then, is to manage this unstable US-China dynamic in a way that harnesses economic
opportunities with Beijing while resolving differences and strengthening its relationship with the US,
with which it has shared interests (India and the US have just inked a 10-year defence framework pact
in Malaysia). New Delhi must also consolidate its partnerships worldwide. Even amid emerging
bipolarity, powers such as Europe, Japan, and Brazil have an important role to play. Ultimately,

questions.stimulus:
Indian democracy has finally matured and now comes with a refund policy. Across parts of Telangana,
defeated candidates in the municipal elections reportedly visited voters to reclaim campaign cash and
gifts, unless the voters could prove that they exercised their constitutional right in favour of the gift-
bearing political Santa. While some may bemoan this as a democratic slide, as an economist, I see a
market correction! For decades, the relationship between candidate and voter resembled festive gifting:


pressure cookers, mixers, saris, and envelopes of goodwill given in the spirit of vague obligations of
reciprocity at the polling booth.


Upfront payment, unverifiable performance, and non-existent enforcement, democracy had its flaws.
From these shadowy, underground markets, we have finally evolved to a transactional era of post-
purchase accountability. Operational questions persist, though – if 3 out of 4 people in the family voted
for the candidate, can they keep the vessel and return only the lid and the whistle? Can there be loyalty
schemes – vote thrice and get a scooty? More importantly, similar consumer rights must be bestowed
upon voters. They must be entitled to warranties, guarantees, and after-sales service. It is only fair.
Democracy cannot operate on a one-sided refund policy. Can every elected representative offer a 12-
month, no-questions-asked return window? If the performance is unsatisfactory, like too much noise,
failure to switch on in assemblies, or unexplained disappearance during crucial sessions, voters may
initiate a replacement.


Political parties must be forced to provide a warranty against manufacturing defects in their ticketed
candidates. Common faults include ideological leakage, sudden policy reversals, chronic absenteeism
and that pervasive, yet mysterious condition called development delays (despite repeated
announcements). Similarly, campaign promises must be treated as advertised product features. Under
the new system, unfortunately for the candidates, promises of pothole-free roads, a reliable supply of
water and power, and corruption-free governance cannot later be classified as “illustrative images
only”. Misleading advertising is actionable under standard consumer law.


The trailblazers in Telangana may have done more than just recover a few pressure cookers. They
have unwittingly elevated democracy onto a higher plane of transparency and accountability with a
clear performance contract – deliver or be returned!

When the GST Council announced a rate rationalisation of the indirect tax regime — which effectively
reduced the tax burden on most goods — it also embraced an opposing dialectic vis-a-vis revenue
collections. On the one hand were the headwinds which would bring down GST collections for the
similar amount of spends on goods and services, and on the other, was an expectation that consumers
would respond to lower tax rates, in effect lower prices, and buy more, leading to a higher tax collection
despite lower tax rates. The government put its faith in the latter. Not only does one have to wait for
the data to be released in December, but one also has to see the trend for the rest of the fiscal year to
ascertain whether some of the demand has just been advanced in the immediate aftermath of the rate
cuts


The monthly GST data for October — it primarily reflects tax collections for business activity in the
month of September — vindicates the government’s belief, for now. The monthly tax collections
number has come in at ₹1.96 lakh crore. The nominal revenue hasn’t fallen in absolute terms compared
to last year, despite strong anecdotal evidence that many consumers deferred purchases for a fortnight
to the period after September 22, when the reduced rates came into effect. There is good reason to
believe that some of the staggered and larger-than-expected (on account of lower taxes leading to lower
prices) purchases would have continued into October as well, and this will show up in the GST data
released in December.


Does this mean the GST rationalisation will necessarily end up as a tailwind rather than a headwind
for overall annual revenue for the current financial year? It is too early to jump to this conclusion
because not only does one have to wait for October data, but one also has to see the trend for the rest
of the fiscal year to ascertain whether some of the demand has just been advanced in the immediate
aftermath of the rate cuts. To be sure, revenue collections, in a large, complex, and diverse
macroeconomy such as India, are always determined by more than one variable. Things such as low
inflation, for example, act as dampers on revenue collection because they represent only a fraction of
nominal income. Similarly, external volatility and its growth headwinds would also weigh down on
income and taxes.

LEGAL REASONING
    (Q.54-Q.58): The Constituent Assembly of India, a body conceived not through direct elections
    but through a complex process of indirect selection, stands as the foundational institution of the
    Indian Republic. Its origins can be traced to the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, which provided
    the framework for its composition and function. The Assembly was tasked with the monumental
    responsibility of drafting a constitution for an independent and diverse nation. Its members, chosen
    by the provincial assemblies through a single transferable vote system, represented a broad cross-
    section of Indian society, including lawyers, freedom fighters, scholars, and political leaders.
    Notably, the Assembly also included a significant, albeit limited, number of women members who
    contributed to the constitutional discourse, numbering fifteen in total.


    The journey of the Constituent Assembly commenced with its inaugural session held in the
    Constitution Hall in New Delhi. This historic first meeting took place on 9 December 1946,
    marking the beginning of a nearly three-year-long deliberative process. With the Muslim League
    initially boycotting the proceedings, the session was attended by 211 members. At this first
    gathering, the need for a presiding officer was paramount. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest
    member of the Assembly, was unanimously elected as its temporary President, or Chairman,
    following parliamentary convention. His role was to preside over the initial proceedings until a
    permanent President could be formally elected, guiding the Assembly through its formative stages
    and the adoption of its inaugural rules of procedure.


    The election of a permanent President occurred shortly thereafter. On 11 December 1946, Dr.
    Rajendra Prasad, a towering figure in the Indian independence movement and a highly respected
    leader, was elected as the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly. He would go on to
    preside over its sessions for the entire duration of the constitution-making process, skillfully
    steering debates and maintaining order among a diverse and often passionately opinionated body.
    Under his stewardship, the Assembly undertook its most critical task: defining the philosophical
    underpinnings of the future Constitution. This was achieved through the Objectives Resolution, a


     momentous document moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946. The Resolution grandly
     outlined the core principles and ideals upon which the Constitution was to be founded, proclaiming
     India as an independent, sovereign republic and guaranteeing its citizens justice, equality, and
     fundamental freedoms. It served as the moral and philosophical compass for the Drafting
     Committee and the Assembly's subsequent deliberations, setting the tone for the entire
     constitutional project.

questions.stimulus:
(Q.59-63): The architecture of any legal system rests upon foundational concepts that define
   authority, entitlement, and capacity. Central to this structure is sovereignty, denoting the ultimate
   authority within a state. Drawing from John Austin and Jean Bodin, the sovereign is the supreme
   law-making power, whose commands are habitually obeyed and who obeys no earthly superior.
   The sovereign is the political superior from whom all positive law emanates, forming the bedrock
   of legal validity.


   From this source flow the fundamental units of analysis: rights and duties. A right is a legally
   protected interest. A crucial distinction exists between legal rights, enforceable by the state, and
   moral rights, grounded in ethics but lacking enforcement. Rights are further categorized by
   substance: positive rights entitle a person to receive something (e.g., education), while negative
   rights entitle one to non-interference (e.g., free speech). By scope, a right in rem is available
   against the world at large (e.g., ownership), whereas a right in personam is available only against
   a specific person (e.g., a contract). Wesley Hohfeld provided the most sophisticated analysis,
   deconstructing rights into four jural correlatives: a claim (enforceable right against another), a
   privilege (liberty to act), a power (ability to alter legal relations), and an immunity (protection
   from another's power). Every right necessarily implies a corresponding duty. A legal duty is an
   obligatory act prescribed by law, whereas a moral duty is a matter of conscience carrying no legal
   sanction.


   These rights and duties can only be held by entities with legal personality—the capacity to have
   rights and duties. This includes natural persons (human beings) and artificial or legal persons. The
   latter category, encompassing corporations and the state itself, is a cornerstone of modern law.
   The concept of corporate personality allows a group to act as a single legal entity, owning property
   and existing independently of its members. A key implication is the veil of incorporation, which
   protects members from personal liability for the corporation's debts.


   Finally, these concepts converge in property law through the distinction between possession and
   ownership. Possession refers to physical control over a thing—a question of fact. Ownership,


      however, is legal title; it is the ultimate right to use and dispose of a thing, recognized by law.
      Ownership takes various forms, including sole ownership, joint ownership, or the division found
      in a trust, where the trustee holds legal ownership for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds
      beneficial ownership. These elements—from the sovereign's command to the beneficiary's
      interest—form the essential vocabulary of jurisprudence, defining the very parameters of legal
      relationships.

(Q.59-63): The architecture of any legal system rests upon foundational concepts that define
   authority, entitlement, and capacity. Central to this structure is sovereignty, denoting the ultimate
   authority within a state. Drawing from John Austin and Jean Bodin, the sovereign is the supreme
   law-making power, whose commands are habitually obeyed and who obeys no earthly superior.
   The sovereign is the political superior from whom all positive law emanates, forming the bedrock
   of legal validity.


   From this source flow the fundamental units of analysis: rights and duties. A right is a legally
   protected interest. A crucial distinction exists between legal rights, enforceable by the state, and
   moral rights, grounded in ethics but lacking enforcement. Rights are further categorized by
   substance: positive rights entitle a person to receive something (e.g., education), while negative
   rights entitle one to non-interference (e.g., free speech). By scope, a right in rem is available
   against the world at large (e.g., ownership), whereas a right in personam is available only against
   a specific person (e.g., a contract). Wesley Hohfeld provided the most sophisticated analysis,
   deconstructing rights into four jural correlatives: a claim (enforceable right against another), a
   privilege (liberty to act), a power (ability to alter legal relations), and an immunity (protection
   from another's power). Every right necessarily implies a corresponding duty. A legal duty is an
   obligatory act prescribed by law, whereas a moral duty is a matter of conscience carrying no legal
   sanction.


   These rights and duties can only be held by entities with legal personality—the capacity to have
   rights and duties. This includes natural persons (human beings) and artificial or legal persons. The
   latter category, encompassing corporations and the state itself, is a cornerstone of modern law.
   The concept of corporate personality allows a group to act as a single legal entity, owning property
   and existing independently of its members. A key implication is the veil of incorporation, which
   protects members from personal liability for the corporation's debts.


   Finally, these concepts converge in property law through the distinction between possession and
   ownership. Possession refers to physical control over a thing—a question of fact. Ownership,


      however, is legal title; it is the ultimate right to use and dispose of a thing, recognized by law.
      Ownership takes various forms, including sole ownership, joint ownership, or the division found
      in a trust, where the trustee holds legal ownership for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds
      beneficial ownership. These elements—from the sovereign's command to the beneficiary's
      interest—form the essential vocabulary of jurisprudence, defining the very parameters of legal
      relationships.

(Q.64-Q.68): Article 17 of the Indian Constitution represents a radical constitutional intervention
    aimed at dismantling the entrenched social evil of untouchability. As a fundamental right, it
    operates not merely as a directive to the state but as an automatic prohibition that renders the
    practice of untouchability illegal from the moment the Constitution came into force. The provision
    declares untouchability abolished and expressly forbids its practice in any form, further mandating
    that any disability arising therefrom shall be an offense punishable in accordance with law. This
    constitutional mandate has been supplemented by parliamentary legislation prescribing specific
    punishments for acts constituting the enforcement of untouchability.


    The judicial interpretation of Article 17 has significantly shaped its scope over the decades. Courts
    have consistently held that the provision is self-executory and operates horizontally, binding both
    state actors and private individuals alike. This means that even in the absence of legislation, the
    practice of untouchability would be unconstitutional. The judiciary has also clarified that the term
    "untouchability" must be construed liberally to encompass any form of social ostracization or
    disability imposed on the basis of birth.


    One of the most significant judicial pronouncements on the subject came in the case of S. P. Mittal
    v. Union of India, where the Supreme Court had occasion to examine the reach of Article 17 into
    the internal affairs of religious denominations. The case arose from controversies surrounding the
    Sri Aurobindo Society and the community at Pondicherry. The Supreme Court addressed the
    scope of Article 17 in relation to the practice of untouchability within religious denominations,


      examining whether customs or usages practiced by religious groups that created social disabilities
      could be struck down as unconstitutional. The Court affirmed that Article 17 overrides any custom
      or usage inconsistent with its provisions, even if such practices claim religious sanction.


      The judgment in S. P. Mittal thus established that no religious denomination can claim immunity
      from the constitutional prohibition against untouchability merely by characterizing discriminatory
      practices as essential to its faith. The Court recognized that while Article 25 guarantees freedom
      of conscience and the right to profess religion, and Article 26 protects the right to manage religious
      affairs, these freedoms are not absolute and must yield to the fundamental right under Article 17.
      This balance reflects the constitutional vision that religious freedom cannot be invoked to justify
      practices that degrade human dignity on the basis of birth. The decision underscores that the
      abolition of untouchability represents a non-negotiable constitutional value that permeates all
      aspects of social life, including the internal workings of religious communities.

(Q.69-Q.73): The stability of treaty relations is a foundational principle of public international
      law, yet the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT) provides mechanisms for both the
      adaptation and orderly dissolution of treaties when circumstances warrant.


      The process of altering a treaty's provisions is governed by the distinction between amendment
      and modification. Under Articles 39-41, amendment refers to a formal change intended to bind all
      parties. In the absence of a specific treaty provision, amendments are generally adopted by the
      same consensus required for the treaty's conclusion, or by an agreed voting mechanism. Once in
      force, an amendment binds all parties, though states that do not ratify it may remain bound by the
      original treaty in their relations with other parties to that original version.


      Distinct from this is modification through inter se agreements under Article 41. This permits some
      parties to a multilateral treaty to modify it as between themselves alone, provided the modification
      is not prohibited, does not affect the rights of other parties, and does not defeat the treaty's object
      and purpose.


      Conversely, the VCLT addresses how treaties may lose their binding force. Under Article 54, a
      treaty may be terminated by consent or in accordance with its own provisions, such as when it
      reaches its expiry date or all parties agree to terminate it. Article 56 addresses denunciation or


      withdrawal from a treaty without a termination clause, permitting it only where implied by the
      nature of the treaty.


      Finally, Article 60 provides that a material breach by one party entitles an injured state to invoke
      it as a ground for suspending or terminating the treaty. In multilateral treaties, a material breach
      allows the other parties, by unanimous agreement, to suspend or terminate the treaty in relations
      between themselves and the defaulting state, ensuring that fundamental violations do not
      undermine the reciprocal obligations upon which the treaty regime is built.

questions.stimulus:
(Q.74-Q.78): The legal framework governing commercial transactions involving movable
   property is encapsulated within the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Section 4 of the Act defines a
   contract of sale as a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods
   to the buyer for a price. The essence of such a contract lies in the existence of two parties, the
   subject matter (goods), and a money consideration. It is imperative to distinguish a ‘sale’ from an
   ‘agreement to sell’. Where property in goods is transferred immediately, it constitutes a ‘sale’.
   Conversely, if transfer is to occur at a future time or subject to a condition, it is an ‘agreement to
   sell’. Furthermore, a contract of sale is distinct from a bailment, as the latter involves only transfer
   of possession, not ownership. Similarly, it differs from a hire-purchase agreement, where
   ownership vests only upon payment of all installments.


   The subject matter is "goods," defined under Section 2(7) as every kind of movable property other
   than actionable claims and money. Goods are classified into three categories. Existing goods are
   owned by the seller at the time of contracting. Future goods are those to be manufactured or
   acquired after the contract. Contingent goods are a type of future goods, the acquisition of which
   depends upon a contingency. Regarding consideration, Section 9 stipulates that the price may be
   fixed by the contract, determined by the course of dealing, or fixed by the valuation of a third
   party.


   A critical aspect involves stipulations regarding quality and title, categorized as conditions and
   warranties. A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose, the breach of which allows
   repudiation. A warranty is collateral, the breach of which gives rise to damages only. The Act
   implies certain terms unless excluded. Key implied conditions include the condition as to title
   (seller has right to sell), sale by description (goods must correspond), sale by sample (bulk must
   correspond), and conditions as to quality or fitness. While caveat emptor (buyer beware) applies,
   exceptions exist where the buyer relies on the seller's skill. Implied warranties include the warranty


     of quiet possession (undisturbed enjoyment), freedom from encumbrances (no third-party
     charges), and quality or fitness by usage of trade.

options.text:

           between ghee and vegetable oil, but cannot return the opened packet for a full refund.

options.label: b

The consumer can reject the goods and claim a refund because there has been a breach of the
           implied condition that goods must correspond with their description.

   knowledge, sells the watch to Kiran, an unsuspecting customer who pays fair market value. Arjun
   discovers the sale and demands the watch back from Kiran. Can Arjun recover his watch?

           owner's rights are permanently extinguished by operation of law.

   market rate as mutually agreed." After three months of successful deliveries with mutually agreed

questions.stimulus:
(Q.79-Q.83): The office of the Vice President of India, established under Article 63 of the
     Constitution, is the second-highest constitutional office in the country. While the Vice President
     serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Council of States, the office also has a
     critical function in the event of a casual vacancy in the office of the President. The framework
     governing the election, powers, and removal of the Vice President is distinct from that of the
     President, reflecting the unique dual role of the office.


     The electoral college for the Vice President consists of the elected and nominated members of
     both Houses of Parliament, voting in accordance with the system of proportional representation
     by means of the single transferable vote. The ballot is secret. To be qualified for election, a
     candidate must be a citizen of India, have completed the age of thirty-five years, and be qualified
     for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. They cannot hold any office of profit under the
     Government of India or any State Government.


     The term of office is five years, and the Vice President may resign his office to the President or
     be removed from office. The process for removal is a formal, political mechanism. A resolution
     for the removal of the Vice President can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha. For the resolution to
     be effective, it must be passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha and agreed
     to by the Lok Sabha. Notably, no formal impeachment process for "violation of the Constitution"
     is prescribed for the Vice President, unlike the process detailed in Article 61 for the President.


     When a vacancy occurs in the office of the President due to death, resignation, removal, or
     otherwise, the Vice President acts as the President until a new President is elected. During this
     period, the Vice President is entitled to the emoluments and privileges of the President and ceases
     to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. In such a scenario, the duties of the
     Chairman are performed by the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

     by means of the single transferable vote. The ballot is secret. To be qualified for election, a

     for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. They cannot hold any office of profit under the
     Government of India or any State Government.

     be removed from office. The process for removal is a formal, political mechanism. A resolution
     for the removal of the Vice President can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha. For the resolution to
     be effective, it must be passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha and agreed
     to by the Lok Sabha. Notably, no formal impeachment process for "violation of the Constitution"
     is prescribed for the Vice President, unlike the process detailed in Article 61 for the President.

     to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. In such a scenario, the duties of the
     Chairman are performed by the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.stimulus:
Rewilding—the large-scale restoration of ecosystems by reintroducing species that have been locally
 extirpated—has moved from the fringes of conservation science to mainstream policy in several
 countries. Its most celebrated examples involve apex predators. When grey wolves were reintroduced
 to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, researchers documented a cascade of ecological changes: elk
 herds began avoiding riverbanks, allowing willows and aspens to recover, which in turn stabilised
 streambeds and increased the diversity of songbirds and beavers. This phenomenon, called a trophic
 cascade, illustrates how a single keystone species can reshape an entire landscape. Proponents of
 rewilding argue that restoring predator-prey dynamics is far more cost-effective than conventional
 conservation management, which often involves intensive, hands-on interventions such as culling
 overpopulated herbivores or manually planting vegetation. Over time, a functioning ecosystem can
 regulate itself, reducing the need for expensive human maintenance. Rewilding advocates also point
 to the psychological and economic benefits of having large, charismatic wildlife—tourism revenues in


 areas with wolf or bear populations have grown substantially in several European nations. Critics,
 however, raise legitimate concerns. Apex predators do not respect park boundaries; wolves and lynx
 have killed livestock in surrounding farmlands, creating conflict with rural communities whose
 livelihoods depend on herding. Compensation schemes exist in some jurisdictions but are considered
 inadequate or bureaucratically cumbersome by affected farmers. There is also a scientific debate about
 whether results from iconic sites like Yellowstone generalise to other ecosystems: some studies have
 found that trophic cascades are weaker or absent in more open, fragmented landscapes. Finally,
 rewilding raises difficult questions about which historical baseline to target. Ecosystems are not static;
 they have changed continuously over millennia, meaning that any chosen reference point is, to some
 degree, arbitrary. The field is evolving rapidly, and most conservation scientists agree that while
 rewilding is a promising tool, it is not a universal solution. [Extracted with revisions and edits from
 academic and policy literature on ecological restoration.]

   reintroduced to Yellowstone. What role does this information play in the argument?

options.label: b

           broader ecological recovery.

options.label: d

questions.stimulus:
Rewilding—the large-scale restoration of ecosystems by reintroducing species that have been locally
 extirpated—has moved from the fringes of conservation science to mainstream policy in several
 countries. Its most celebrated examples involve apex predators. When grey wolves were reintroduced
 to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, researchers documented a cascade of ecological changes: elk
 herds began avoiding riverbanks, allowing willows and aspens to recover, which in turn stabilised
 streambeds and increased the diversity of songbirds and beavers. This phenomenon, called a trophic
 cascade, illustrates how a single keystone species can reshape an entire landscape. Proponents of
 rewilding argue that restoring predator-prey dynamics is far more cost-effective than conventional
 conservation management, which often involves intensive, hands-on interventions such as culling
 overpopulated herbivores or manually planting vegetation. Over time, a functioning ecosystem can
 regulate itself, reducing the need for expensive human maintenance. Rewilding advocates also point
 to the psychological and economic benefits of having large, charismatic wildlife—tourism revenues in


 areas with wolf or bear populations have grown substantially in several European nations. Critics,
 however, raise legitimate concerns. Apex predators do not respect park boundaries; wolves and lynx
 have killed livestock in surrounding farmlands, creating conflict with rural communities whose
 livelihoods depend on herding. Compensation schemes exist in some jurisdictions but are considered
 inadequate or bureaucratically cumbersome by affected farmers. There is also a scientific debate about
 whether results from iconic sites like Yellowstone generalise to other ecosystems: some studies have
 found that trophic cascades are weaker or absent in more open, fragmented landscapes. Finally,
 rewilding raises difficult questions about which historical baseline to target. Ecosystems are not static;
 they have changed continuously over millennia, meaning that any chosen reference point is, to some
 degree, arbitrary. The field is evolving rapidly, and most conservation scientists agree that while
 rewilding is a promising tool, it is not a universal solution. [Extracted with revisions and edits from
 academic and policy literature on ecological restoration.]

questions.stem:
The author states that choosing a historical baseline for rewilding is "to some degree, arbitrary."
   Which of the following would, if true, most directly undermine the significance of this concern?

options.label: a
options.text:
Scientists have confirmed that all ecosystems have remained completely unchanged for at
           least the past two thousand years, eliminating baseline uncertainty.

options.label: b
options.text:
Rewilding practitioners have developed target-free frameworks that focus on restoring
           ecological processes and functional diversity rather than any fixed historical species
           composition.

options.label: c
options.text:
Archaeological evidence shows that apex predators were absent from most European
           landscapes for longer periods than they were present, complicating restoration goals.

options.label: d
options.text: Both A and B are true, and together they eliminate the baseline problem entirely.

questions.stimulus:
Algorithmic tools that assist judges in sentencing and bail decisions have proliferated across the United
 States and are beginning to appear in other jurisdictions. These tools—often called risk assessment
 instruments—generate a score predicting the likelihood that a defendant will reoffend or fail to appear


 in court. Proponents argue that replacing subjective judicial intuition with data-driven analysis reduces
 arbitrary variation in sentencing and provides a more consistent, transparent basis for decisions. The
 most prominent criticism concerns fairness. A 2016 investigation by ProPublica found that one widely
 used tool, COMPAS, assigned higher risk scores to Black defendants than to white defendants with
 comparable criminal histories. The company that developed COMPAS disputed the methodology, and
 a subsequent debate among statisticians revealed that the fairness criteria being applied were
 mathematically incompatible with each other: it is impossible to simultaneously satisfy all common
 definitions of algorithmic fairness when base rates of reoffending differ between groups. This is not a
 flaw that better data or more sophisticated modelling can resolve—it is a structural tension. A second
 concern involves transparency and due process. Most commercial risk assessment tools are
 proprietary, meaning defendants cannot inspect the algorithm used to evaluate them. Several courts
 have ruled that this does not violate constitutional protections, but legal scholars argue that individuals
 have a right to understand and challenge evidence used against them. If the inner workings of a tool
 are a trade secret, that right is effectively nullified. Supporers counter that human judges are also
 biased and inconsistent, and that the relevant question is not whether algorithms are perfect but whether
 they perform better than the baseline they replace. They also note that risk scores are advisory, not
 determinative—judges retain the final decision. The debate ultimately reflects a deeper tension
 between the desire for efficiency and consistency in the justice system and the principle that
 punishment must be individualised and contestable. [Extracted with revisions and edits from academic
 and policy literature on algorithmic governance.]

options.label: a
options.text:
The passage presents a single, unambiguous argument in favour of algorithmic sentencing
           tools and systematically dismisses all counterarguments.

options.label: b
options.text:
The passage presents a factual scenario, identifies two major criticisms, notes a defence
           offered by proponents, and concludes by framing the issue as a deeper normative tension.

options.label: c
options.text:
The passage uses the ProPublica investigation as its main conclusion and treats everything
           else as supporting premises.

options.label: d
options.text:
The passage argues that algorithmic tools should be abolished and replaced entirely by human
           judicial discretion, supported by evidence from constitutional law.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument that risk assessment tools
   reduce bias compared to unaided judicial decision-making?

options.label: a
options.text:
A meta-analysis of sentencing data finds that jurisdictions using risk scores show no
           statistically significant reduction in racial disparities in sentencing outcomes compared to
           jurisdictions that rely solely on judicial discretion.

options.label: b
options.text:
Legal scholars have proposed a model algorithmic fairness statute that would require all risk
           assessment tools to be open-source and publicly auditable before use in courts.

options.label: c
options.text:
Several high-profile cases have emerged in which judges overrode low risk scores to impose
           harsh sentences, suggesting that the tools are being used inconsistently.

options.label: d
options.text:
Both A and C, taken together, suggest that the tools neither reduce bias nor are applied
           consistently, undermining both justifications for their use.

questions.stem:
The passage notes that judges retain final decision-making authority even when risk scores are
   provided. What is the most reasonable inference from this fact in the context of the passage's
   argument?

options.label: a
options.text:
This fact fully resolves the due process concern because defendants can always appeal to the
          judge's independent judgment rather than relying on the algorithm.

options.label: b
options.text:
This fact partially addresses one concern about algorithmic determinism but does not resolve
          questions about transparency, since the score may still influence a judge even if it is technically
          advisory.

options.label: c
options.text:
This fact confirms that risk assessment tools have no real impact on sentencing outcomes,
          making the entire controversy largely academic.

options.label: d
options.text:
This fact demonstrates that the structural tension between efficiency and individualisation is
          irresolvable and that algorithmic tools should therefore be banned.

A legal reformer argues: "Defendants should have the right to inspect and challenge any risk
   score used in their case; this requires that all such tools be publicly available and independently
   auditable." Which of the following best identifies the underlying principle that this argument relies
   on?

options.label: a
options.text:
Criminal punishment should be swift and uniform, and any tool that achieves this goal is
           justified regardless of its transparency.

options.label: b
options.text:
Procedural fairness requires that individuals be able to examine and contest evidence or
           evaluations used against them in legal proceedings.

options.label: c
options.text:
Risk assessment tools are inherently more accurate than human judgment and should therefore
           be made mandatory in all sentencing decisions.

options.label: d
options.text:
Both A and C together form the basis of the reformer's position.

Direction (115-120): Study the following information carefully and answer the questions given below.

A small retail shop in Delhi deals in electronic accessories such as earphones, chargers, and power
banks. During the festive season, the shopkeeper decided to offer discounts to increase sales while still
maintaining a reasonable profit margin.

He purchased a batch of 200 earphones at a cost price of Rs.150 each. To attract customers, he marked
the price 40% above the cost price. However, due to competition in the market, he offered a discount
of 20% on the Marked price. Despite the discount, he noticed that some defective pieces had to be sold
at an additional loss of 10% on their cost price. Out of the total stock, 20 earphones were defective.

Meanwhile, the shopkeeper also sold chargers. He bought 100 chargers at Rs.270 each and sold them
at a marked price that ensured a profit of 25% even after giving a discount of 10%. All chargers were
sold successfully without any defect.

At the end of the season, the shopkeeper calculated his overall profit or loss from both products. He
realized that while discounts helped increase sales volume, the defective items slightly impacted his
overall earnings.
questions.stem: What was the total Cost Price (CP) for the entire batch of 200 earphones?

Direction (115-120): Study the following information carefully and answer the questions given below.

A small retail shop in Delhi deals in electronic accessories such as earphones, chargers, and power
banks. During the festive season, the shopkeeper decided to offer discounts to increase sales while still
maintaining a reasonable profit margin.

He purchased a batch of 200 earphones at a cost price of Rs.150 each. To attract customers, he marked
the price 40% above the cost price. However, due to competition in the market, he offered a discount
of 20% on the Marked price. Despite the discount, he noticed that some defective pieces had to be sold
at an additional loss of 10% on their cost price. Out of the total stock, 20 earphones were defective.

Meanwhile, the shopkeeper also sold chargers. He bought 100 chargers at Rs.270 each and sold them
at a marked price that ensured a profit of 25% even after giving a discount of 10%. All chargers were
sold successfully without any defect.

At the end of the season, the shopkeeper calculated his overall profit or loss from both products. He
realized that while discounts helped increase sales volume, the defective items slightly impacted his
overall earnings.
